readerTitle: Eleven jobs, time for six: what do you drop?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (바닥재 매장 겸 시공 업체: 소매·유통 + 가정 서비스) · 하나로 이어지는 시뮬레이션 · 인물과 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 일이 넘칠 때 필요한 것은 더 오래 버티는 힘이 아니라 무엇을 빼고, 맡기고, 미룰지 정하는 판단이다. 가장 먼저 밀려나는 일은 대개 급하지 않지만 가장 중요한 일이다.
misconception: 과부하는 체력과 의지로 버티면 해결된다. 미뤄도 당장 문제가 없는 일이 가장 먼저 뺄 일이다.

sources.text: 시간 관리의 표준 원리 (긴급성과 중요성 구분, 위임, 집중 시간 확보)
모든 인물, 업체, 일정은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 인물과 일정은 가상입니다. 2번 카드 목록은 7개 항목이지만 그중 '팀 회의·급여·이메일'을 여러 일로 묶었습니다. 제목의 '11개 일'과 맞는지 게시 전에 확인하세요. 필요하면 제목 숫자를 조정하세요.
'아침 시간에 집중력이 가장 높다'는 모든 사람에게 해당하지 않습니다. 카드에서는 Dana 개인의 패턴으로만 썼습니다. 일반 법칙처럼 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.
하루 반을 확보한다는 추정(재고 조사 위임 + 강연 거절 + 출시 연기)은 설명용 어림값입니다.

cards.title: Eleven jobs, time for six: what do you drop?
body: Monday, 7:40 a.m. Dana owns a flooring business: a showroom and warehouse that sell tile and wood, plus a crew that installs floors in people's homes.
This week has more work than hours. Her usual fix is to work later. Let's see if there's a better one.

image.label: A shop owner at a counter facing a long sticky-note list
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 이른 아침 바닥재 매장 카운터에서 커피를 든 여성 사장이 벽에 빽빽하게 붙은 포스트잇을 바라봄. 뒤로 타일 샘플 진열대와 창고 선반이 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Everything on Dana's plate
body: Here is what Dana has to get done by Friday:
list: Place the spring order with her main tile supplier. **Prices lock Friday.**
Fix a kitchen install that's running late. The customer is angry.
Run the quarterly stock count in the warehouse
Interview two installer candidates. She's been short-staffed for months.
Approve the new online store before its launch date
Give a talk at the local trade association
cards.callout: Her plan, as always: do it all, late into the night.
cards.softwareNote: A software team's version of this week: a release, a customer escalation, a hiring loop and a conference talk. The thinking that follows works the same way.

cards.title: Where does Dana start?
body: She has one coffee and an hour before the shop opens.

options.text: Start right away and work evenings until it's all done
options.feedback: She might finish, but tired people make costly mistakes, and the supplier order is the worst place to make one. It also teaches her team that the plan is simply that Dana stays late.

options.text: Spend 20 minutes sorting by impact and deadline, and mark what only she can do
options.feedback: Twenty minutes buys a clear view. The supplier order and the angry customer are urgent and important. Hiring is important but not urgent. The talk is neither.

options.text: Clear the quick tasks first to shrink the list
options.feedback: Ticking items off feels like progress, but quick tasks are rarely the ones that matter. By Thursday the supplier order is still waiting.

cards.title: Say you chose to sort. Now something has to go.
body: Even sorted, the list is about a day and a half too long. What does Dana drop, hand off or delay?

options.text: Hand the stock count to her warehouse lead, delay the online store a week, decline the talk
options.feedback: She frees about a day and a half. Her warehouse lead has counted stock before, a week's delay costs little, and the talk can wait until next quarter.

options.text: Postpone the interviews. Hiring can wait.
options.feedback: It's the easiest item to push because nothing breaks this week. That's exactly why it's been pushed for months, and why she's overloaded now.
It saves an hour, but the meeting is where she hands off work. Cutting it can make the overload worse.

cards.title: Say you chose to hand off and delay. When does the supplier order happen?
body: Pricing the spring order takes Dana about two hours of careful thinking. She knows she's sharpest early and flat by mid-afternoon. The visit to the angry customer will take a lot out of her too.

options.text: Tuesday, 8 to 10 a.m., phone off, before the shop opens
options.feedback: Her hardest thinking gets her best hours. The customer visit goes after lunch, where a calm conversation matters more than sharp math.

options.text: Thursday evening, once everything else is done
options.feedback: She'd work on it tired, with no slack left if the supplier pushes back before Friday's deadline.

options.text: In short bursts between other tasks all week
options.feedback: It gets done eventually, but every restart costs focus. Detailed pricing needs one long, quiet stretch.

cards.softwareNote: The same rule protects deep work on a product team: block the hardest design or coding work in your sharpest hours and put meetings around it.

cards.title: Say you chose the morning block. Friday: done, just.
body: The order is in and the customer is calmer. But next month looks just as full. What does Dana do now?

options.text: Ask her warehouse lead and her install lead: "What do I hold onto that you could take?"
options.feedback: They see what she can't. She double-checks orders that were already checked, and she prices quotes the install lead could price. Their answers point to work she can hand over for good.

options.text: Promise herself to say no more often
options.feedback: The intention is good. But without knowing which yeses cost the most, it usually fades within a few weeks.
A new tool organizes the same pile. The problem isn't where the list lives. It's what's on it.

cards.title: Dropping work has costs too.
body: Declining the talk may cost a useful contact. Delaying the online store may disappoint someone who planned around it. So say it early and plainly: what's moving, why, and the new date.
And if every week looks like this one, better sorting isn't the real fix. The business needs fewer commitments or another person. That's why the hiring stayed on the list.

image.label: Three trays labeled Do, Hand off, Delay
image.brief: 플랫 인포그래픽. 책상 위 서류함 세 칸에 "Do", "Hand off", "Delay" 라벨. 옆에 쓰레기통 대신 "Say no" 라벨이 붙은 작은 상자. 각 칸에 2번 카드의 일 이름이 적힌 카드가 꽂혀 있음.

cards.title: Overload is a sorting problem before it's a stamina problem.
body: Each of Dana's decisions used an idea from this unit:
list: **Sort before you start** · Managing your time
**Drop low-value work, not the important work that can wait** · Managing your time
**Give hard thinking your best hours** · Managing your energy
**Ask others what you hold onto** · Asking for feedback
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write your week's list. Mark one item to hand off and one to drop, then tell the people affected.
